questions.question: Differentiate between hazardous and non-hazardous compounds in e- waste with examples. / [CO1]
questions.solution_html:
• Differentiate hazardous vs non-hazardous compounds in e-waste with examples.
  • Definition of hazardous and non-hazardous compounds-3 marks
  • Examples-2 marks
  • E-waste contains a variety of materials that can be classified as hazardous and non-hazardous
  • based on their chemical composition and impact on the environment and human health.
  • Hazardous compounds:
  • These are substances that pose serious risks due to their toxic, corrosive, or flammable nature.
  • Common examples include:
  • - Lead (Pb): Found in solder, cathode ray tubes (CRTs), and circuit boards; can cause
  • neurological damage.
  • - Mercury (Hg): Present in switches, fluorescent lamps, and flat screens; causes kidney and brain
  • damage.
  • - Cadmium (Cd): Used in batteries and semiconductors; a known carcinogen.
  • - Brominated flame retardants (BFRs): Present in plastic casings and cables; persistent organic
  • pollutants (POPs).
  • Non-hazardous compounds:
  • These materials are generally stable and pose minimal direct health risks. Examples include:
  • - Plastics (PVC, ABS): Used for insulation and casings.
  • - Glass: Found in monitors and screens.
  • - Metals like iron, aluminum, and copper: Recyclable and valuable for recovery.
  • Proper segregation of hazardous and non-hazardous components is crucial for safe handling,
  • recycling, and environmental protection.

questions.question: Discuss one major limitation of paper-based dielectric materials in electronics. / [CO2]
questions.solution_html:
• Discuss one major limitation of paper-based dielectric materials in electronic
  • applications.
  • Definition of paper based dielectric material-2 marks
  • Limitations ( Any 3)- 3 marks
  • Paper-based dielectrics are lightweight, biodegradable, and low-cost materials that have attracted
  • attention in flexible and sustainable electronics. However, they have significant limitations that
  • restrict their large-scale application.
  • The major limitation of paper-based dielectric materials is their poor moisture resistance and low
  • dielectric stability under humid or high-temperature conditions. Paper is inherently hygroscopic
  • — it absorbs moisture from the environment, leading to:
  • - Reduced dielectric strength and insulation resistance.
  • - Swelling and dimensional instability.
  • - Increased dielectric losses and short circuits.
